DEFENDANTS’ MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO EXCLUDE PLAINTIFF’S EXPERT, RONALD H. WHARTON MD, UNDER FED. RULE OF EVID. 702 Defendant JOpen, LLC (“Defendant” or “JOpen”) hereby files this Motion to Exclude Plaintiff’s Expert Witness, Ronald H. Wharton, MD, under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993) and the incorporated memorandum of law. I. INTRODUCTION Dr. Wharton’s opinions—that the decedent, Harmony Moller, died from a cardiac event induced by kratom—are inadmissible for three reasons. Plaintiff intends to present Dr. Ronald Wharton—a cardiologist with no background in toxicology, pharmacology, kratom research, or forensic pathology—to tell a jury that kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death. But under controlling Fifth Circuit precedent, an expert must be qualified in the subject matter of his opinion, must establish general causation before offering specific causation, and must apply a reliable methodology at every step. Dr. Wharton satisfies none of those requirements. 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 22 First, he is not qualified to opine on kratom’s toxic effects. He had never studied kratom, treated kratom exposure, researched kratom pharmacology, or encountered it clinically before this litigation. Rule 702 does not permit a cardiologist to step into the role of toxicologist simply because the case involves a heart. Second, his causation theory collapses at the threshold. The Fifth Circuit requires proof of a harmful level of exposure before general causation may be presented to a jury. Dr. Wharton admits he does not know what a safe dose of mitragynine is, what a lethal dose is, or what exposure level is capable of causing fatal arrhythmia. Without that foundation, specific causation cannot proceed. Third, his “process of elimination” is not a reliable differential diagnosis. He failed to investigate critical medical history, failed to account for numerous other substances, failed to review key materials, and relied on assumptions rather than verified facts. The Fifth Circuit prohibits that kind of post hoc reasoning. Daubert requires intellectual rigor—not speculation, not litigation-generated hypotheses, and not conclusions reached because the expert “can’t think of anything else.” Because Dr. Wharton’s testimony fails Rule 702 at each step—qualification, general causation, and specific causation—it must be excluded in its entirety. II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND On February 6, 2023, 36-year-old Harmony Moller was found dead in her home. Ex. 1 (November 18, 2025 Expert Report of Dr. Ron Wharton) (“Initial Report”), at 1. Ms. Moller’s cause of death was listed as an “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine use.” Id. A toxicology report confirmed the presence of mitragynine at a level of 150 ng/mL in her femoral blood. Id. 2

III. ARGUMENT A. Standard for admissibility. The district court has considerable discretion to admit or exclude expert testimony under Fed. R. Evid. 702. See Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 138–39 (1997); Seatrax, Inc. v. Sonbeck Int’l, Inc., 200 F.3d 358, 371 (5th Cir. 2000); Tajonera v. Black Elk Energy Offshore Operations, LLC, Civ. A. No. 13-0366, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8 (E.D. La. June 7, 2016) (Brown, J.) (citing authority). The burden rests with the party seeking to present the testimony to show that the requirements of Rule 702 are met. Moore v. Ashland Chemical, Inc., 151 F.3d 269, 276 (5th Cir. 1998). Rule 702 provides that an expert witness “qualified . . . by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion” when the following requirements are met: 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 22 (a) The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Rule 702 codifies the Supreme Court’s opinion in Daubert, which charges district courts to act as “gatekeeper” when determining the admissibility of expert testimony. Tajonera, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8. The purpose of a Daubert motion is “to ensure that only reliable and relevant expert testimony is presented to the jury.” Rushing v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 185 F.3d 496, 506 (5th Cir. 1999) (superseded by rule on other grounds) (citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 590–93). When an injury was allegedly caused by a substance, the Fifth Circuit applies a two-step framework to examine the admissibility of causation evidence. Knight v. Kirby Inland Marine, Inc., 482 F.3d 347, 351 (5th Cir. 2007). First, the court must determine whether there is admissible evidence of general causation: that “a substance is capable of causing a particular injury.” Id. Second, if the court “concludes that there is admissible general-causation evidence, [it] must determine whether there is admissible specific-causation evidence.” Id. Critically, “[e]vidence concerning specific causation . . . is admissible only as a follow-up to admissible general-causation evidence.” Id. The Court’s inquiry is whether the expert’s reasoning is reliable at each step. Knight, 482 F.3d at 355. Opinions based on assumptions, speculation, or gaps between the data and the conclusion are inadmissible. Id.; Viterbo v. Dow Chem. Co., 826 F.2d 420, 424 (5th Cir. 1987). 10

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 11 of 22 The proponent must prove admissibility by a preponderance, and “expert’s assurances” do not substitute for objective reliability. Moore, 151 F.3d at 276. B. Dr. Wharton is not qualified to offer his causation opinions in this case. Dr. Wharton is a cardiologist. He is not trained in toxicology, pharmacology, forensic pathology, or kratom research. Yet, he proposes to tell a jury that kratom’s active compounds caused a death. That opinion is outside his expertise, outside his training, and outside the limits Rule 702 imposes on expert testimony. Rule 702 does not allow a witness to leverage general medical credentials into authority over an entirely different scientific field. An expert “may not go beyond the scope of his expertise in giving his opinion.” MGMTL, LLC v. Strategic Tech. Inst., Inc., 2022 WL 485279, at *6 (E.D. La. Feb. 17, 2022) (Vitter, CJ). Dr. Wharton does precisely that by offering opinions on the specific chemical properties of mitragynine and its effect on the human body—a subject he knew nothing about before this litigation, and still does not, as demonstrated in his deposition. His lack of expertise in the relevant fields is the first of many reasons his testimony should be excluded. See Moore, 151 F.3d at 276. In Moore, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the exclusion of an expert based on the district court’s conclusion that the bases for their opinion was “individually and collectively inadequate” under Daubert. Id. at 277. The excluded expert’s “training and experience . . . were obviously important to his diagnosis” but he “gave no reason why these items were helpful in reaching his conclusion on causation” and “admitted that he had never previously treated a patient who had been exposed to a similar Toluene solution” – the solution that was alleged to cause the harm. Id. at 277–78. The Court noted the excluded expert “was a highly qualified pulmonary specialist, but, as the Seventh Circuit observed in Rosen v. Ciba-Geigy Corp., 78 F.3d 316 (7th Cir. 1996), “[u]nder the regime of Daubert a district judge asked to admit scientific evidence must determine whether the 11

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 12 of 22 evidence is genuinely scientific, as distinct from being unscientific speculation offered by a genuine scientist.” Id. at 318 (internal citation omitted).” Dr. Wharton is an accomplished cardiologist, whose expertise is in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a condition he opines Harmony Moller did not have and did not contribute to her death. Defendant is not challenging Dr. Wharton’s expertise as a cardiologist or Dr. Wharton’s qualifications to testify about the impact of Harmony Moller’s “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff” or whether or not she had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. But Dr. Wharton has no knowledge, skill, experience of training in the core issues here: kratom, and its toxicology and pharmacology, and its ability to cause or contribute to death. Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 27:4–28:15, 70:3-17, 100:3-7. He expressly admitted he is not a medical toxicologist or pathologist. Id. at 27:4–28:15, 67:18-70:5. During his deposition on February 23, 2026, the profound deficiencies in Dr. Wharton's qualifications and methodology became clear. Dr. Wharton was not “familiar with kratom prior to receiving this case.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 46:25–47:23. He has never done any research on kratom, never treated any patient for kratom exposure and never encountered kratom in his clinical practice. Id. His “opinions on kratom in this case are based solely on the articles and references that [he] cited in his [his] report.” Id. at 59:7-11. To supplement his kratom knowledge he acquires information from the internet (e.g. on the “profit margin” on kratom) and is prepared to testify on those topics based solely on this research, when it is not his “job” “to give [] a set of references.” Id. at 62:5–65:25; 137:6-21. Dr. Wharton demonstrates a complete lack of knowledge on kratom products generally. He incorrectly referred to the O.P.M.S. Silver Products at issue as liquids and extracts – when they are pure kratom ground leaf material. He has no knowledge regarding how 7-OH is synthetically in 12

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 13 of 22 kratom products. He testified that the presence of 7-OH in Harmony Moller’s autopsy is important to his opinion, but the coroner findings do not refer to any quantifiable level of 7-OH, nor is there any. This is precisely the kind of expert overreach Daubert is designed to prevent. A cardiologist may testify about cardiac structure and disease. He may not step into the role of toxicologist simply because the case involves a heart. Dr. Wharton admitted he had never studied kratom, never treated a kratom exposure, never researched its pharmacology, and learned about it only after being retained for this case. Allowing him to testify anyway would present the jury with the imprimatur of medical authority untethered to actual expertise. Rule 702 requires more than credentials—it requires qualification in the subject at issue. Because Dr. Wharton lacks that qualification, his kratom causation opinions must be excluded. C. Dr. Wharton failed to establish general causation before opining on specific causation. Even assuming Dr. Wharton is qualified to address cardiac physiology, his general- causation opinions are independently inadmissible under Rule 702. Fifth Circuit precedent requires reliable scientific evidence identifying a harmful level of exposure before causation testimony may be presented to a jury. Dr. Wharton concedes that no such dose is known here. That failure is dispositive. The Fifth Circuit requires admissible general-causation evidence before any specific- causation testimony may be admitted. Johnson v. Arkema, Inc., 685 F.3d 453, 469 (5th Cir. 2012); Knight, 482 F.3d at 351. At a minimum, general causation requires scientific knowledge of a harmful level of exposure. Johnson, 685 F.3d at 469; Allen, 102 F.3d at 199. Dr. Wharton must therefore identify “the harmful level of exposure” to mitragynine that is capable of causing a fatal arrhythmia in the general population. Kaoui v. BP Expl. & Prod., Inc., No. CV 17-3313, 2023 WL 13

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 14 of 22 330510, at *2 (E.D. La. Jan. 12, 2023) (Vitter, CJ), 2023 WL 330510, at *6. He has not, because he cannot. He admitted he does not know what constitutes either a safe or lethal dose. Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 71:22–72:25. Dr. Wharton acknowledged that his opinion is “based on reasonable speculation” and “his experience as a cardiologist” as “[w]e have no hard data on a drug or agent of this nature.” Id. at 167:10–170:21. Dr. Wharton claims that scientific literature suggests a “linkage between the main alkaloid in Mitragyna speciosa (kratom) use, ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation) and cardiorespiratory adverse events” and “potentially fatal effects on the electrocardiogram attributed to the use of kratom.” Ex. 1, Initial Report, 2–3. This opinion fails to establish general causation for several reasons. First, as noted above, the one article he cites for his opinion concludes “a lack of a convincing mechanistic link between mitragynine and ventricular arrhythmia” and state “causal determinations cannot be made.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 191:7-194:12. Thus, the study does not identify the harmful level at which physical symptoms manifest though that was an object of the study. Thus, Dr. Wharton fails to cite evidence of general causation. Kaoui, 2023 WL 330510, at *6 (“To establish general causation, a causation expert must identify ‘the harmful level of exposure to a chemical’ at which physical symptoms manifest.”). This Court has stressed, “nearly every chemical on Earth may be toxic or even fatal at a certain level of exposure,” so “[c]ausation experts determine not only whether a chemical is capable of causing certain health effects, but at what level of exposure do those health affects appear.” Id. “[F]ailure to properly identify the level of exposure to a particular chemical at which harmful effects occur necessarily renders a general causation opinion to be unreliable and, thus, inadmissible.” Id. 14

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 15 of 22 Dr. Wharton’s opinion on general causation is therefore unreliable and thus inadmissible because he fails to identify any evidence of a fatal dosage of kratom. See also, Moore, 151 F.3d at 277–79 (affirming district court’s exclusion of expert where he had “no information on the level of exposure necessary for a person to sustain the injuries about which the MSDS warned. The MSDS made it clear that the effects of exposure to Toluene depended on the concentration and length of exposure.”). Where assumptions substitute for facts—such as, for example, exposure, as here—causation devolves into “mere guesswork” and is inadmissible. Seaman v. Seacor Marine L.L.C., 326 F. App’x 721, 727–28 (5th Cir. 2009) (affirming exclusion where assumptions about exposure levels rendered causation opinion “mere guesswork” and failed to establish either general or specific causation). Even assuming Dr. Wharton is qualified in his own field, his general-causation opinions must be excluded because they fail the Fifth Circuit’s most basic reliability requirement: identifying a scientifically established harmful level of exposure. D. Dr. Wharton's specific causation opinion is unreliable. Even if Dr. Wharton could establish general causation—which he cannot—his specific causation opinion independently fails under Rule 702 because it rests on a fundamentally unreliable “process of elimination.” He admitted that he concluded kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death because he “can’t think of anything else that would have done this.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 218:10–14. That is not science. It is guesswork. 1. The Fifth Circuit has rejected this exact methodology. An expert may eliminate alternative causes only after establishing that the substance at issue is capable of causing the injury and only if the elimination itself is performed in a scientifically reliable manner. Where either step fails, the opinion is inadmissible. 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 16 of 22 Dr. Wharton characterizes his method as a “differential diagnosis,” which he agrees requires systematically eliminating “any other possible cause.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 248:14– 249:24. But the Fifth Circuit has made clear that process-of-elimination reasoning is not admissible unless it is anchored in reliable scientific groundwork. In Black v. Food Lion, Inc., the Fifth Circuit excluded expert testimony where the expert concluded that because she had ruled out other possible causes, the remaining event “had to be” the cause. 171 F.3d 308, 313 (5th Cir. 1999). Id. The Court explained, “This analysis amounts to saying that because [the expert] thought she had eliminated other possible causes of [the condition], even though she does not know the real ‘cause,’ it had to be the [injury-causing event]. This is not an exercise in scientific logic but in the fallacy of post-hoc propter-hoc reasoning.” The Fifth Circuit further held that such a “general methodology cannot vindicate a conclusion for which there is no underlying medical support.” Id. at 314. That is precisely what happened here. Dr. Wharton does not identify a scientifically established harmful dose of mitragynine. He does not establish a validated mechanism of death tied to a known exposure level. Instead, he assumes kratom must be responsible because he does not see a better explanation. That is the same reasoning rejected in Black. A differential diagnosis is not a free pass. It is admissible only when the expert reliably establishes general causation and then methodically rules out alternatives based on complete and accurate data.
